analytic.title: P-FRP Task Scheduling: A Survey

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) is a declarative approach for modeling and building reactive systems. The FRP has been shown to be an expressive formalism for building graphics, robotic, and vision applications. The Priority-based FRP (P-FRP) is a formalism of FRP that allows preemption of execution and guarantees real-time response. Since functional programs cannot maintain state and mutable data, changes made by programs that are preempted have to be rolled back, and the work done by the preempted programs has to be discarded. Hence in the P-FRP model, a preempted lower priority task will have to restart after higher priority tasks have completed execution. Current real-time research mainly focuses on the classic preemptive or non-preemptive models and plenty methods have been developed to analyze the real-time guarantees of these models. Unfortunately, due to its transactional nature where preempted tasks are aborted and have to restart, the execution semantics of the P-FRP model does not fit into the standard definitions of classic preemptive or non-preemptive execution. In this survey paper, we review existing researches on the P-FRP task scheduling, and present a few research areas for future work.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the implementation of computer systems there are two distinct types of programming paradigms available, imperative and functional. In the imperative or procedural style of programming, computation is performed by changing states based on a sequence of instructions. Several real-time systems are implemented using the imperative style of programming using C/C++, Java, or Ada.

In contrast to the imperative style, the functional or declarative style of programming treats computation as an evaluation of mathematical functions and avoids use of state and mutable data. The functional programming style focuses on a concise definition of a problem and not on the correct sequence of actions that will lead to the desired solution. While imperative programming paradigm has its own merits, the absence of state and mutable data in functional programs makes them immune to side-effects. The functional paradigm provides the guarantee that a program or routine will only compute its results and not have unintended consequences on other programs. This leads to a considerable reduction in bugs and leads to high quality software, a vital consideration in safety and mission-critical systems. Another benefit of functional paradigm is that since they do not have state and mutable data, no shared variables are used thus making them ideal for concurrent computing. An excellent comparison of functional and imperative programming style using practical example is available in John Hughes' paper [28]. Since the formal system of λ-calculus (lambda-calculus) was first devised by Church [21] and Kleene [34], many functional programming languages have been invented: LISP, Ocaml, Haskell, Scheme, Erlang, F#, Atom, Scala and so on. Haskell and Erlang have been studied and commercially developed intensively. Scala is recently adopted by companies such as Linkedin, Twitter and Walmart [42]. Nowadays, computer applications are becoming more and more interactive, driven by all sorts of events that originate from within the applications and their outside environment. The reactive programming paradigm has been recently proposed as a solution to develop such event-driven applications, graphics, robotic, and vision applications for instances. Bainomugisha et al. [4] conduct a comprehensive survey on reactive programming. Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) [43] is a framework for constructing reactive applications using the building blocks of functional programming. Hudak et al. [27] presented Yampa as an instantiation of FRP as a domain-specific language embedded in Haskell.

div.head: A. Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP)
div.p: In real-time systems, the correctness of a program is measured by its logical output as well as its ability to complete within certain time limits. FRP is demonstrated to be effective in modeling and building reactive systems such as graphics, robotic and vision applications. However, another significant feature of real-time systems, priority, is not considered in FRP. To address this problem, the Priority-based FRP (P-FRP) [32] model has been proposed as a variant of the FRP model.

The P-FRP model supports assigning different priorities to different events, and higher priority events can preempt lower priority ones. However, to maintain guarantees of type safety and stateless execution, the functional programming paradigm requires the execution of a function to be atomic in nature. To comply with this requirement, as well as allow preemption of lower priority events, the P-FRP implements a transactional model of execution. Using only a copy of the state during event execution and atomically committing these changes at the end of execution, the P-FRP model ensures handling an event in a way of "completion or nothing", and thus maintains both the type-safety and the state-less execution paradigm of the FRP, and does not require the use of synchronization mechanisms between tasks in the system. It has the potential to transform the building of more complicated Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs). The impact of P-FRP in building safer controllers in automobile anti-lock brake systems has been demonstrated in Christoffersen and Cheng [20].

In the P-FRP model, the transactional execution scheme is also called the Abort-and-Restart (AR), which is a scheme [32] to support the P-FRP, and we also use the P-FRP model or the AR model as the short form of the P-FRP AR model. In the classic preemptive model, the lower priority tasks continue their execution from where they are preempted. It is, however, different in the P-FRP model that when the lower priority tasks are preempted their executions are aborted and restart as new after the higher priority tasks have finished execution. The task scheduling in the classic preemptive model and the P-FRP AR model are shown in Fig. 1.

Past research in real-time computing for the classic model has focused on systems implemented using imperative programming, which are generally classified under preemptive and non-preemptive systems. Due to its stateless nature of computation, the execution semantics of the P-FRP model is different from classic preemptive and non-preemptive execution and existing state-of-the-art methods developed by realtime researchers for the classic model cannot be applied for ascertaining real-time guarantees in the P-FRP. In this work, we summarize the existing researches on temporal aspects of the P-FRP model.

div.head: B. Copy and Restore Operation
div.p: In the P-FRP AR model, when a task starts processing it creates a "scratch" state, i.e., a copy of the current state of the system. Changes made during the processing of this task are maintained inside such a state. When the task has completed, the "scratch" state is restored into the final state in an atomic operation. During the restoration and copy operations the task being processed cannot be preempted by higher priority tasks. If a task is preempted after copy but before the restore operation, the scratch state is simply discarded. The contextswitch between tasks only involves a state copy operation for the task that will be commencing processed.

div.head: C. Organization
div.p: Research of P-FRP task scheduling falls into following three categories: priority assignment, schedulability, and response time analysis. This review paper is organized as follows. Section II gives basic concepts and notations; Section III presents the research of priority assignment; Section IV presents schedulability and response time analysis; Section V presents research of modified models other than the native AR scheme of the P-FRP model; Section VI concludes the paper and presents some future research directions in the model.

div.head: II. BASIC CONCEPTS AND NOTATIONS
div.p: We consider a fixed priority hard real-time uni-processor system in the P-FRP model with n independent periodic tasks Γ n = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n }. In such task systems, each task τ i is assigned a unique fixed priority i (1 ≤ i ≤ n), where 1 is the highest priority and n is the lowest.

An instance or invocation of a task is called a job. J k i refers to the k th job of τ i . Each periodic task τ i is characterized by a (maximum) computation time C i , a constant arrival time period T i between two successive jobs of the task, a relative deadline D i (D i ≤ T i ), and a release offset (or phasing) Φ i . Release offset Φ i is the time, relative to time 0, when the first job is released by task
div.formula: τ i . Let Φ {k} min = min k i=1 {Φ i }, and Φ {k} max = max k i=1 {Φ i }.
div.p: Utilization of each task is U i = C i /T i , and the total utilization of the task set is U = ∑ n i=1 U i . Let LCM k = LCM (T 1 , T 2 , ..., T k ) denote the Least Common Multiple (LCM, or hyperperiod) of the periods of the first k highest priority tasks, 1 ≤ k ≤ n, and LCM 1 = T 1 . Without loss of generality, we assume 0 < C i ≤ min {D i , T i } for all i, 1 ≤ i ≤ n. t copy (k) is the time taken to make a copy of the state before τ k starts execution, and t restore (k) is the time taken to commit the state after τ k has completed execution. Thus the total process time of τ k is
div.formula: P k = t copy (k) + C k + t restore (k).
div.p: In real-time scheduling, Integer Time Model means that temporal parameters are measured by counting the number of clock cycles, hence temporal values have a resolution of one clock cycle. In this paper all temporal parameters are thus assumed to be non-negative integer values, and all values of i, j, k, m, and n are positive integer values. It is also assumed that a task can only be preempted at discrete (integer) time instants.

For a given priority assignment, a task set Γ n satisfying the basic phasing condition refers to that it satisfies 0≤Φ i < T i for all i, 1≤i≤n. For a given priority assignment (GPA), a task set Γ n satisfying the initial busy condition [30] refers to the following condition: For each i, 2≤i≤n, min 1≤j<i {Φ j }<
div.formula: Φ i + C i and Φ i ≤ max 1≤j<i {Φ j +R GP A j,1 }, where R GP A j,1
div.p: is the response time of the first job of task τ j for the GPA.

There are three constraint levels on task relative deadlines studied in the literature [23], [22]. For all i, 1≤i≤n, implicit deadlines implies D i =T i , constrained deadlines having D i ≤T i , while arbitrary deadlines means that task deadlines may be less than, equal to, or greater than their periods. The response time R j i of the j th job of a task τ i is the time between the release of a job and its completion. The response time R i of a task τ i at a given release offset pattern is the maximum one of all R j i . The Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) of a task is derived under the worst-case release pattern that leads to the largest interference on the considered task. Such a particular scenario is often referred to as the critical instant [36].

Periodic task sets may be synchronous if there is some time point at which all tasks arrive at the same time, or be asynchronous where all tasks never arrive simultaneously. Tasks with common release must be synchronous. However, tasks with different release offsets do not imply they are asynchronous tasks, since they may arrive at the same time in the future. For example, when all task periods are co-prime, the task set must experience a common release, regardless of any imposed offsets [1][3]. Notice that for an asynchronous scheduling there may still be some tasks (but never all) sharing a common release.
A feasibility interval is a time interval [t, t + H) such that if all tasks are schedulable in the interval [t, t + H) then the tasks will also be schedulable in the time interval [0, Z) :
div.formula: Z → ∞ [35],[1]. A schedulability testing interval [a, b) is a time interval in which the schedulability of a given task set is checked. In general, the length of [a, b) is no less than that of [t, t + H).
div.p: In scheduling theory, a non-work-conserving scheduling is the one that may let the CPU stay idle even when there are tasks ready for execution, while a work-conserving one does not. Fully preemptive scheduling allows a running task to be interrupted whenever a higher priority task releases. Fully nonpreemptive scheduling does not allow a running task to be interrupted by other tasks for any reason. There are scheduling algorithms in between fully preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling algorithms. For example, they set portions of a task preemptive and the rest non-preemptive.

In existing research work for the P-FRP model, it is usually assumed that tasks are independent and there is no precedence constraints between tasks, i.e., tasks cannot be blocked from execution by another task except contending for a processor. Therefore, lock-free and wait-free data sharing have not been considered in the P-FRP model. It is also assumed that once a job starts to execute it will not suspend itself.

div.head: III. PRIORITY ASSIGNMENT IN THE P-FRP MODEL
div.p: To date, researchers have studied several priority assignment algorithms for P-FRP tasks.

div.head: A. Rate Monotonic, Utilization Monotonic, or Deadline Monotonic Priority Assignments
div.p: In [8], [9], Belwal and Cheng proved that the Rate Monotonic (RM) and the Utilization Monotonic (UM) priority assignments are generally not optimal in the AR model, where RM priority assignment sets a higher priority to a task with a smaller task period (i.e., faster arrival rate) and UM priority assignment orders tasks non-increasingly by task utilization ratios. For 2-task sets, however, the RM and the UM are optimal when one task period is at least two times of the other, and for n-task sets where n > 2 the RM priority assignment is optimal only for the case that task periods are harmonic (i.e., integer multiples of each other) and different. Notice that a task with a smaller task period is not necessarily having a larger utilization ratio, for example, a 2-task set with C 1 = 1, T 1 = 3, and C 2 = 2, T 2 = 4, where U 1 = 1/3 and U 2 = 1/2. Notice also that, as stated in [9], under some restrictions RM or UM priority assignment may be optimal in the P-FRP model.

In the classic preemptive model, for periodic task sets with constrained deadlines and scheduled asynchronously, the Deadline Monotonic (DM) priority assignment is generally not optimal, where DM priority assignment orders tasks nondecreasingly by task relative deadlines. In [30], Jiang et al. proved that negative propositions in the classic preemptive model remain negative in the P-FRP model. Therefore, for the same constraints, the DM priority assignment is also generally not optimal in the P-FRP model.

div.head: B. Utilization-and-Rate Monotonic
div.p: A priority assignment being U-RM property, i.e., both utilization and rate monotonic, is referred to as the Utilizationand-Rate Monotonic (U-RM) priority assignment, which was mentioned in the paper given by Belwal and Cheng [8], [9]. The idea of the U-RM priority assignment is that a task is assigned with a higher priority if it has a larger utilization ratio and smaller task period. Clearly, this priority assignment is only applicable to task-sets that have the U-RM property. In general this will not be the case.

div.head: C. Execution-time Monotonic
div.p: Wong and Burns [44], [45] introduced the Execution-time Monotonic (EM) priority assignment, which assigns a higher priority to a task τ i which has a larger computation time C i . Since the EM is not optimal, they derived an improved priority assignment named the Execution-time-toward-Utilization Monotonic (EUM) priority assignment scheme. EUM priority assignment starts with EM ordering and the worst-case is when a task set can only be scheduled by UM ordering (or is not schedulable at all, by only fails at the last task). The lower priority tasks shift up with higher priority level one by one until the task-set is in UM ordering. They showed that the EUM dominated both EM and UM. However, the EUM is also not optimal for the P-FRP model.
In summary, there is still no optimal priority assignment discovered for general P-FRP tasks at present.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS IN THE P-FRP MODEL
div.p: In this section, we discuss fixed priority scheduling for P-FRP tasks. To ensure a system meets all deadlines in the real world, a schedulability test is required for the task-set in the system. In Burns and Wellings' book [6], four characteristics are defined for testing schedulability: Necessary, Sufficient, Exact, and Sustainable. Specifically, a necessary test means that if a task-set fails the test it will miss at least one deadline; A sufficient test means that if a task-set passes the test it will meet all deadlines; An exact test means both characteristics of sufficient and necessary; A Sustainable test means that a task set maintains schedulable if conditions for scheduling have been improved (e.g., by reducing the utilization of a task).

In the classic preemptive model [36], a sporadic task can be viewed as a periodic one with a minimum arrival time period for schedulability test or response time analysis without changing the schedulability. This is, however, generally not the case in the P-FRP model. Wong and Burns [44], [45] showed that a sporadic task with a later release may bring a longer response time. This property implies that in the P-FRP model when a sporadic task set is treated as periodic and is schedulable it is not necessarily schedulable when treated as sporadic. Therefore, in this paper sporadic tasks will not be considered unless otherwise stated.

div.head: A. Critical Instant
div.p: A critical instant for a task means the time at which a release of that task will lead to the longest response time. The motivation for finding the critical instant is that when scheduling a task-set, we need to determine the worst-case response time to check if the task-set is schedulable.

In fixed priority scheduling with the classic preemptive model, Liu and Layland [36] proved that a task is at its critical instant when the task and all higher priority tasks are released at the same time (synchronous release). Unfortunately, Belwal and Cheng [7], [9] showed that in the P-FRP model a synchronous release of tasks is not necessarily lead to the worst-case response time.

Moreover, Jiang et al. [30] observed that in the P-FRP model under fixed priority scheduling both synchronous and asynchronous periodic task sets are not necessarily schedulable even if all of the first jobs of tasks can meet their deadlines, and furthermore, the response time of the first job of any task is also not necessarily to be the WCRT, which are different from that in the classic preemptive model. Considering all possible release-time and abort combinations, Wong and Burns [44], [45] showed that finding the critical instant for the AR model with periodic and sporadic tasks is intractable. We argue that in the P-FRP model whether there is generally a critical instant or not has not been proved and if the answer is "yes" the problem of how to find the critical instant efficiently remains also open.

div.head: B. Feasibility Interval
div.p: In the P-FRP model, Belwal et al. [19] presented the first result on the feasibility interval and showed that, for a schedulable n-task set Γ n under fixed priority scheduling, the feasibility interval of Γ n is [t, t + LCM n ), where t ≥ Φ {n} max . However, it does not hold for some scenarios. Specifically, the interval [Φ {n} max , Φ {n} max +LCM n ) is not a feasibility interval for some scenarios. Jiang et al. [29] presented an algorithm to calculate the minimal schedulability testing interval for tasks with arbitrary release offsets. They first employed S i by
div.formula: S 1 = Φ 1 , S i = max{Φ i , Φ i + ⌈(S i-1 -Φ i )/T i ⌉ × T i }, 2 ≤ i ≤ n [26],

div.head: C. Necessary Tests
div.p: It is known that a necessary test is in fact a property that a model possesses. It is known that for uni-processor n-task systems a simple necessary test is that the total utilization factor of the task set is at most 1, i.e., U ≤ 1. This property holds for both the classic preemptive model and the P-FRP model, under fixed or dynamic priority assignment. Since it provides little information on unschedulable task sets which still satisfy U ≤ 1, the test is of more importance in the theoretical sense than in the practical sense.

Currently, in the P-FRP model few necessary tests are discovered. In [30], Jiang et al. presented that for a periodic task set under a fixed priority assignment, a necessary schedulability test in the P-FRP model is that it is schedulable for the same priority assignment in the classic preemptive model. As stated in [9], there were also some necessary tests for P-FRP tasks satisfying some special restrictions.

div.head: D. Sufficient Tests
div.p: Sufficient tests are more powerful for schedulability test. As shown in [36], in the classic preemptive model for an n-task set, a sufficient schedulability test is U = n(2 1/n -1) under fixed priority scheduling, and a sufficient schedulability test is U ≤ 1 (being also a necessary test as shown above) under Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling. It is, however, not necessarily the case in the P-FRP model. This is because that in the classic task system the total processing time in a time period is fixed once the tasks are given, while in the P-FRP model the total processing time is changed at run time due to that the restarting discards the incomplete execution, which is equivalent to adding some processing time into the task system. Therefore, this-like utilization-based sufficient test is generally not applicable to P-FRP tasks, though under some restrictions there can also be some utilization-based sufficient tests, for example, a utilization bound 1/n proposed in [10].
As for non-utilization-based sufficient tests, there were some sufficient tests for P-FRP tasks satisfying some special restrictions [9].

Moreover, for periodic P-FRP tasks satisfying basic phasing and initial busy conditions under a given priority assignment, Jiang et al. [30] proposed somewhat general and efficient simulation-based sufficient tests for both synchronous and asynchronous tasks, and by the sufficient tests the schedulability is only needed to be checked with an optimal search length LCM n-1 , the least common multiple of the first n -1 higher priority task periods, instead of LCM n . It is worthy of stating that the sufficient tests are also applicable to sporadic tasks due to that they are simulation-based tests.

div.head: E. Exact Tests
div.p: Actual response time analysis (RTA) [31] is an "exact" schedulability test based on calculating the worst-case response time of a task which includes the time of interference from other higher priority tasks and blocking from lower priority tasks (due to shared resources or non-preemptive scheduling). RTA is not exact unless blocking is exact.

Since it is still unknown whether there is optimal priority assignment for an n-task set in the P-FRP model, existing researches pay first attention to calculating the longest response time under a given priority assignment. If the longest response time of a task is longer than its deadline, the task will not meet its deadline. The opposite situation is that if the longest response time of the task is less than or equal to its deadline, the task will meet its deadline. The analysis can be applied for arbitrary deadlines. Several methods to compute the exact response time for the P-FRP model are given by researchers. Notice that except for exhausted permutation of priority assignment ((n -1)! for an n-task set) the so-called worst-case response time results derived in existing P-FRP literatures are indeed longest response time under some given priority assignment since currently there is still no optimal priority assignment discovered for general P-FRP tasks.

div.head: 1) Iteration-based Response Time Analysis:
div.p: A natural way to make response time analysis (RTA) in the P-FRP model is to extend the famous fixed point iteration algorithm developed by Audsley et al. [2]. Considering extra costs incurred due to the abort of tasks, Ras and Cheng [39] presented the first RTA expression for computing approximate response time bounds in the P-FRP model. However, the expression failed to converge for some scenarios [9] and therefore was an unreliable method to obtain guaranteed results. Belwal et al. [17] introduced a O(N 2 ) polynomial time algorithm that computes an approximate upper bound on the response time. The experimental analysis showed that the quality of the bound given by this algorithm varies significantly.

Wong and Burns [44], [45] presented a new iterative expression for calculating response time in the P-FRP model. We find, however, that their new expression is also unable to give correct result for some scenarios, for example, a synchronous 3-task set with implicit deadlines and task parameters are
To the best of our knowledge, there is at present still no effectively iterative expression for calculating response time in the P-FRP model.

2) Gap-Enumeration Method: Time-Accurate Simulation (TAS) [11] is a simple way to calculate the response time in the P-FRP model. The approach is to execute a simulation through each time unit within the feasible interval. Aiming to improve the efficiency, the Gap-Enumeration Method (GEM) [11] which enumerated k-gaps was used for reducing the time complexity for a calculation of response time analysis in the P-FRP model. The idea is that there is a time slot which is first allocated with the highest priority task and second with the next higher priority task and so on. When a task is fitted, the response time for the task is found. If the task τ i cannot find a gap, it will miss its deadline. The gap-search function can be simply explained in that it searches the first k-gap which is fitted with the size of P k . The authors use a red-black tree (RB-tree) in their experiments. In the P-FRP model, the first job of τ i meets the deadline but that does not mean other jobs of τ i will meet deadlines because a synchronous release may not lead to a critical instant. It remains an open question as to whether the Gap-Enumeration Method is sufficient if there is no critical instant.

3) Idle-period Game Board Algorithm: Belwal and Cheng [12] thought that the GEM was hard to program because an RB-tree was not available as a native function in pro-gramming languages. Another technique using a game board was an easier way because the method can be implemented by using a simple array. Moreover, they changed the term Gap-Enumeration to idle-period. This Game Board Algorithm (GBA), however, was essentially the same as the GEM.

div.head: 4) Longest Response Time through Time Petri Nets:
div.p: Belwal et al. [18] developed Time Petri Net (TPN) models for schedulability analysis in the P-FRP model. A publicly available TPN tool called ROMEO [25] was used. In the experiment, 50 task sets of sizes varying from 2 to 4 tasks were synthetically generated. The execution times for these task sets were selected from the range [5,15], while their arrival periods were selected from [30,100]. On the same platform with an Intel dualcore machine and Microsoft Windows Vista, the exhaustive enumeration took an average of 1, 8 and 20 minutes to run the simulation of 2, 3 and 4-task sets respectively. The queries on TPN models using ROMEO obtained the result with a 3 to 4 seconds delay for a few 4-task sets.

div.head: 5) LList-based exact test:
div.p: The above simulation-based methods are in fact exhaustive-search-based methods for response time and schedulability analysis. Moreover, for an ntask set a test interval with at least a length LCM n , the least common multiple of all n task periods, was required. It is obviously inefficient for larger LCM n .

Lv et al. [38] present a linked list-and simulation-based exact test method for the classic preemptive model under fixed priority scheduling. The preliminary results have shown that the LList-based exact test is a good candidate in exact response-time tests when task periods span no more than three orders of magnitude. Notice that this method is also applicable to the P-FRP model and this is one of their current work. Furthermore, in [30], Jiang et al. have obtained and proved an optimal search length LCM n-1 instead of LCM n for n-task sets satisfying the basic phasing and the initial busy conditions for a given priority assignment in the simulationbased exact response time calculation and schedulability test. This is the current best result on the problem.

div.head: F. A Case Study for the P-FRP AR model
div.p: In [39], Ras and Cheng presented also their case study for the P-FRP AR model. Two cases are studied in software and on hardware. The authors use the Generic Avionics Platform [37] task set in their case studies. In the first study, they evaluated the AR model under RM and EDF scheduling and then compare the results with other models such as nonpreemptive, Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [41], and Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [5]. Another study was for hardware: the Analog Devices' ADuC814 micro-controller was used to run the P-FRP compiled code with RM and EDF scheduling. The result of this case study was the number of tasks against the average number of aborts and the average number of aborts against system load.

div.head: G. Multi-processor scheduling
div.p: Based on their previous work [39], Ras and Cheng [40] derived inequalities for calculating response time upper bound of a task in a symmetric multi-processor (SMP), under RM and EDF scheduling respectively. This is the first attempt extending the AR model to SMP systems.

Belwal and Cheng [13] presented off-line partitioning of tasks in SMP system in order to find the minimum number of processors required to feasibly schedule the tasks in a given P-FRP task set. The authors implemented three first-fit based heuristics: P-FRP First-Fit-Decreasing Rate, P-FRP First-Fit-Decreasing Utilization Factor and P-FRP First-Fit-Decreasing Processing Time. Unlike previous works where theoretical proofs to validate the performance of the first-fit algorithms are derived, the authors only used experimental tasks sets for the heuristics' comparison and validation.

div.head: V. ALTERNATIVE MODELS IN THE P-FRP
div.p: It is obvious that the restarting in the AR model wastes the executed time (we call it the abort cost) and therefore the schedulability would benefit from reducing the number of preemptions (aborts). Alternative models are proposed to improve the of P-FRP tasks.

div.head: A. Software Transactional Memory in the P-FRP
div.p: Software transactional memory (STM) is a transactional mechanism of controlling access to shared resources in memory. This transactional mechanism is similar, but also distinct, to the AR scheme in the P-FRP model and thus allowing results in the P-FRP model to be adaptable for the analysis of STM.

Belwal and Cheng [14] presented Timed Automata encodings that can be used for schedulability analysis in the STM model. The TA models were implemented in the model checker UPPAAL and used in the schedulability analysis of experimental task sets. By using the tool UPPAAL which provides algorithms for state space search for reachability analysis, the schedulability of a task set can be ascertained in a much more efficient way to the method of exhaustive enumeration. In the experiment, the parameters of tasks were purposely kept small to reduce the time taken in exhaustive enumeration. Totally, 50 task sets each having 2 to 4 tasks were synthetically generated, and the execution times for these task sets were selected from the range [3,12], while their arrival periods were selected from [15,60]. Even with such small numerical values, it took approximately 5 to 20 minutes (the machine used was an Intel dual-core machine running Windows XP), to derive the WCRT for the lower priority task in each set. By contrast, schedulability analysis through Timed Automata in UPPAAL took time from 2 to 8 seconds.

In [15], [16], Belwal and Cheng presented also some properties, necessary tests, and sufficient test for the real-time software transactional memory-lazy conflict detection (STM-LCD) model. Zhou et al. [47] studied also on the worst case response time and schedulability analysis for real-time STM-LCD model. They introduced a parameter, the remainder factor m; formally derive an exact WCRT for 2-task sets on STM systems using lazy conflict detection (LCD) and proposed an exact schedulability test for 2-task sets. Also, they presented a near-exact WCRT for n-task sets on STM-LCD, and proposed a new necessary condition and a new sufficient condition to schedule n-task sets.

div.head: B. Deferred Abort
div.p: Inspired by the Deferred Preemption (DP) technique [6], which combines the techniques of preemptive and nonpreemptive execution and is designed for non-atomicexecution systems being unable to be directly applied to the P-FRP model, Wong and Burns [46] proposed the P-FRP Deferred Abort (DA) model (shortened as the DA model). In the DA model, a task was divided into two regions: the first region was AR and the second region was non-preemptive and nonabortable. The motivation of the DA model was to reduce the number of preemptions by eliminating some unnecessary preemptions. The definition of unnecessary aborts is that if a higher priority task does not abort a lower priority task, the system can still be schedulable.

div.head: C. Deferred Start
div.p: Zou et al. [48] proposed a non-work-conserving model, Deferred Start (DS), for P-FRP systems to reduce the number of preemptions by postponing the start of a job. Consider the facts that the classic preemptive model, the classic nonpreemptive model, the P-FRP AR model, and the P-FRP DA model have the following properties, respectively:

1) In the classic preemptive model, when a task is running and a higher priority task releases and takes control of the processor, the lower priority task pauses execution. And when the lower priority task gets again control of the processor, it resumes from the point where it was paused; the alreadyexecuted part of the task remains effective.

2) In the classic non-preemptive model, once a task, whatever its priority is, starts executing, no task can interrupt it. Each successfully scheduled task thus occupies a continuous block of time at the length of the task's execution time. Nonpreemptive scheduling raised a problem that was called priority inversion. When priority inversion happens, tasks with higher priorities have to wait for the completion of the tasks with lower priorities.

3) In the P-FRP AR model, a newly released higher priority task interrupts the running task instantly in the same way it does in the classic preemptive model. However, for the interrupted task, it must start from the beginning whenever it is given control of the processor again. No matter how many times a task is interrupted and how much processor time it has spent in the uncompleted executions, there has to be a continuous block of time no shorter than the length of the task's execution time in order to let it finish execution. This AR model can also be called the fully-AR model. 4) In the P-FRP DA model, a task contains two regions: preemptive and non-preemptive. It works in the preemptive region in the same way as the P-FRP AR model does, and works in the non-preemptive region in the same way as the classic non-preemptive model does.

Zou et al. [48] stated that there are incomplete execution regions for an individual task in both the classic preemptive model and the P-FRP model. The difference is that the incomplete execution regions of the same task in the classic preemptive model are valid towards the final complete execution of the task, while those in the P-FRP model are not.

In fact, these incomplete executions have no effect on the completion of tasks in the P-FRP model. So there are two steps leading to the P-FRP DS model from the P-FRP AR model. Formally, there are two steps. In the first step, DS uses "idle" periods to replace the incomplete execution regions in the AR scheduling, and in the second step, without affecting the execution of tasks with higher priorities, DS moves backward the complete execution of a lower-priority task if it fits in an "idle" period. By repeating the second step for tasks from the second highest-priority task (no need for the highest-priority task) to the lowest-priority task, DS derives the schedule of the P-FRP task sets. Notice that there can be different implementations corresponding to different fitting policies, such as first-fit, last-fit, best-fit, etc., for the DS model.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS
div.p: In this short survey, we reviewed existing researches on P-FRP task scheduling. Due to the abort-and-restart nature of the P-FRP model, existing research results of the classic model are usually unable to be applied directly to the P-FRP model. The P-FRP model is a promising solution to address the needs of more complicated CPS systems and many questions remain open and deserve for further research.

div.head: 1) Work-Conserving Model:
div.p: For fixed priority periodic P-FRP task scheduling, whether there are critical instant and optimal priority assignment or not remain open. Finding more efficient non-simulation-based schedulability tests and analyzing worst-case response time deserve more research efforts. The schedulability and response time analysis problems under non-fixed priority scheduling policies, such as EDF, as well as those dealing with arbitrary deadlines are also future work. Considering the blocking time, release jitter, sporadic tasks, robustness during overloads, resource sharing, and task interactions deserve also further study. Most these-like questions on multi-processor systems remain also open.

2) Non-Work-Conserving Model: Considering the complexity of the P-FRP model, we think that domain-specific research in which task sets with special parameters are more realistic and practical than the generalized ones in this stage. We also think that alternative models are worthy of study. The P-FRP DS model is the first non-work-conserving model for the P-FRP, and we will explore further its properties and applications with respect to domain-specific problems.

3) Memory-aware Scheduling: Existing P-FRP schedulability and response time research do not consider the memory/cache effect of restarted tasks. Kazemi and Cheng [33] presented their preliminary study of the P-FRP task execution time on a scratchpad memory-based platform, and showed that the task execution time changes because of the memory hierarchy. Zou and Cheng [49] proposed their preliminary results on memory aware response time analysis for P-FRP tasks. Simulation results showed that the schedulability and response time were improved when considering different execution time of a task in cases of start and restart. More theoretical response time analysis and priority assignment research in memory aware P-FRP task scheduling are needed. Also, since the execution time difference is likely related to data placement/locality, memory aware scheduling has more impacts on multiprocessor scheduling.
